title: Tuple
description: Read a tuple as one complete fact, understand attribute bindings and identity, and handle optional SQL values without losing rows.
notes:
## One tuple expresses one fact

A tuple is one element of a relation. It supplies a value for every attribute in the relation's schema. In Student(student_id, student_name, programme, score), a displayed tuple such as (17, Asha, Computing, 86) associates four values with four named roles. The tuple represents one student fact under this schema. The relation is the collection of all such facts, rather than another name for this individual tuple.

Always ask what one tuple means in its own relation. In Enrollment(student_id, course_id, enrolled_on), one tuple represents a student's enrollment in one course. A student enrolled in several courses has several enrollment tuples. Those tuples do not imply several student identities. Confusing the grain of different relations leads to incorrect counts, inappropriate uniqueness constraints, and accidental deletion of legitimate repeated participation.

## Attributes give values their roles

The displayed position of a value is useful only when the schema's attribute order is known. In (17, Asha, Computing, 86), the final number means score because that is the displayed fourth attribute. Without the schema, the number might instead mean age, credits, or an identifier. A value alone cannot explain its role, measurement scale, or permitted range.

An attribute-based description is clearer: student_id is 17, student_name is Asha, programme is Computing, and score is 86. The logical fact associates values with names. Rearranging columns together with their corresponding values does not change those associations. Swapping the values while keeping the names fixed can change the fact or make it invalid. Presentation order and attribute meaning are different concerns.

## Every tuple follows the same structure

The relation's degree determines how many attribute values each tuple has. If Student has four attributes, each Student tuple has four attribute positions. A row with a missing optional score in SQL still has the score column; NULL marks the absence of an ordinary value in that position. It does not shorten the row or reduce the relation's degree.

SQL INSERT syntax can omit columns that have suitable defaults or permit NULL. The database constructs a complete stored row according to the table definition. Omitting a required column without an acceptable default may fail. Therefore an INSERT statement listing three expressions does not prove the resulting four-column table contains a three-attribute tuple. Distinguish the statement's supplied inputs from the completed row defined by the schema.

## Complete equality and business identity

Two strict relational tuples are equal when their values agree for every corresponding attribute. Matching names alone is insufficient: two students named Asha can have different identifiers. A set-based relation cannot contain two copies of the same complete tuple. Practical SQL tables can permit repeated rows unless relevant constraints prevent them, so inspect the actual definition before assuming uniqueness.

A candidate key identifies a tuple using a subset of attributes. If student_id is a key, its value must identify at most one Student tuple. Two rows with identifier 17 and different names are different complete rows but violate that key rule. This distinction matters when cleaning data: SELECT DISTINCT over all columns does not repair contradictory facts associated with one intended identity.

## Position is not an identifier

A tuple does not acquire its identity from being the third row on a screen. The same facts can be displayed in another order without changing the relation. Storage movement, query planning, and a changed sort expression can all change a row's observed position. Applications should identify the intended record through a key rather than through an offset into an unordered result.

For example, an update to student 17 should constrain student_id, not assume the first displayed Asha is the intended student. Names can repeat, and display order can change. A key-based condition expresses the fact being targeted. Before updating a real dataset, preview the condition's matches and consider transaction and authorization requirements; a syntactically valid statement can still target the wrong population.

## SQL NULL needs a separate interpretation

Classical relational descriptions use domain values. SQL extends practical row handling with NULL and three-valued comparison behaviour. A NULL score can mean the score has not been recorded, if that meaning is defined by the application. It is different from a recorded zero. Replacing every missing score with zero changes the represented facts and can distort averages, rankings, and eligibility decisions.

A SQL row containing multiple NULLs is still one row if the schema permits those absences and all other constraints hold. NULL is forbidden in a primary key and in a NOT NULL column. Other constraints can also reject a proposed row. Never infer validity merely from the row's width: structural completeness and satisfaction of integrity rules must both be considered.

## Filtering tuples without losing optional facts

WHERE retains rows whose predicate evaluates to TRUE. FALSE and UNKNOWN do not pass the filter. A comparison such as score >= 80 excludes a row with a NULL score because the comparison is unknown. Use IS NULL when the task specifically asks for missing scores. Use an explicit alternative when both high scores and missing scores must appear.

```sql
SELECT student_id, student_name
FROM students
WHERE score IS NULL
ORDER BY student_id;
```

The query returns one output row for every matching student. It keeps the identifier so that two students with the same name remain distinguishable. Removing student_id and adding DISTINCT would answer a different question: which distinct names occur among students with missing scores. That might hide separate students who require separate follow-up actions.

## Projection creates output tuples

A query can construct result tuples with fewer attributes or computed attributes. Selecting student_id and score produces output rows of degree two even if the source has degree four. That does not modify stored Student tuples. Similarly, an expression such as score + 5 produces a computed result value; it does not update the stored score without an appropriate data modification statement.

Name computed columns descriptively so readers understand their meaning. A query can classify a score as missing, passing, or below the threshold with CASE. Put the missing-value branch explicitly in the expression when the output contract distinguishes absence. Otherwise an ELSE branch can silently mix missing scores with recorded failing scores, even though those states require different student support actions.

## Counting rows and recorded values

COUNT(*) counts rows in a group. COUNT(score) counts rows whose score expression is non-NULL. With three student tuples and one missing score, the counts are three and two respectively. Neither count is the number of attributes. If a join repeats a student once per enrollment, COUNT(*) over that joined result counts enrollment combinations rather than automatically counting distinct students.

Build a tiny fixture before trusting a report: include two students sharing a name, a recorded zero, a missing score, and a high score. Check the population retained by each predicate and the meaning of each output column. These examples expose assumptions about identity and absence that a dataset of unique names and complete positive scores would never challenge.

## Reviewing a tuple-based solution

Read a proposed tuple against the named attributes, check domain compatibility, and then check key and cross-row rules. For SQL, also check nullability and the handling of unknown comparisons. Decide whether the output must preserve each source identity or intentionally collapse selected values. Specify an order only when the presentation or automated comparison requires one, using a tie-breaker where necessary.

The useful idea is precise and small: one tuple is one structured fact in a particular relation. Its values are meaningful through attributes, its admissibility depends on constraints, and its identity should not depend on where it happens to appear. Carrying that interpretation into SQL makes filters, computed results, counts, and targeted updates easier to explain and verify.

questions.question_text: What does a tuple represent within a relation?
options: A single column definition
One fact binding a value to each named attribute in the relation schema
The name of the relation
The total count of rows in the relation
questions.explanation: A tuple binds values to attributes; its displayed positional order must be interpreted using the schema.

questions.question_text: In Students(id, name, department, gpa), how many values does each tuple contain?
options: 4, one for each attribute
It varies from tuple to tuple
questions.explanation: Every tuple in a relation has exactly as many values as the relation's degree (number of attributes) — here, 4.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly distinguishes a Tuple from a Relation?
options: A tuple is a whole table; a relation is one row
A relation is the entire set of tuples; a tuple is one element (row) of that set
They are exactly the same concept
A tuple contains multiple relations
questions.explanation: A relation is the set; a tuple is a single member (row) belonging to that set.

questions.question_text: Can the same relation legally contain two tuples with identical values in every attribute?
options: Yes, always
No, because a relation is a set and cannot contain duplicate elements
Only if the primary key is NULL
Only for relations of degree 1
questions.explanation: Since a relation is a set, two tuples with identical values in every attribute would be the same set element, not two distinct tuples.

questions.question_text: Under Students(id, name, department, gpa), what does 9.1 represent in (3, Meera, CS, 9.1)?
options: The degree of the tuple
The value the 'gpa' attribute takes for this specific tuple
A separate relation
The cardinality of the relation
questions.explanation: 9.1 is simply the value bound to the 'gpa' attribute within this one tuple/row.

questions.question_text: Does the physical position of a tuple among other tuples in a relation carry logical meaning?
options: Yes, tuple order determines its identity
No, tuple order is meaningless since a relation is an unordered set
Only for the first tuple inserted
Only in relations with a primary key
questions.explanation: Because relations are sets, no ordering among tuples is logically significant.

questions.question_text: In an SQL Students table that permits NULL in department and gpa, and whose other constraints hold, is (5, Ganesh, NULL, NULL) one valid row?
options: No, tuples cannot contain more than one NULL
Yes, it is one well-formed tuple even though two of its values are NULL
No, NULL values are not permitted in tuples at all
Yes, but it counts as two tuples
questions.explanation: The SQL row remains one row; permitted NULLs do not remove columns. Actual validity also depends on all other table constraints.

questions.question_text: If a relation's degree is n, what can you say about every tuple belonging to that relation?
options: Each tuple has exactly n values, one per attribute
Each tuple has at most n values
Tuples may vary in size up to n
n refers to the number of tuples, not values per tuple
questions.explanation: Degree fixes how many attributes the schema has, and every tuple must supply exactly that many values.

questions.question_text: A four-column SQL row contains a NULL score. How many attribute positions does it have?
options: Three
Four
Zero
One per non-NULL column only
questions.explanation: NULL does not remove the score column.

questions.question_text: Two students share a name but have different identifiers. What follows?
options: They must be one tuple
The name is necessarily a key
They can be distinct tuples
One must be deleted
questions.explanation: Complete identity cannot be inferred from a repeated name.

questions.question_text: Why should an update target a student identifier rather than a screen row number?
options: Rows always stay at fixed disk positions
Keys guarantee authorization
Display position can change while a key identifies the intended fact
Screen numbers are always unique forever
questions.explanation: Logical identity must survive reordered results.

questions.question_text: A four-column table is queried with SELECT student_id, score. What is the output degree?
options: Four
The number of students
Zero
Two
questions.explanation: The output tuple contains two selected attributes.

questions.question_text: Three rows include one NULL score. What are COUNT(*) and COUNT(score)?
options: 3 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 3
2 and 2
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(expression) excludes NULL results.

questions.question_text: What does WHERE score >= 80 do to a row with NULL score?
options: Include it as zero
Exclude it because the predicate is UNKNOWN
Raise a compulsory error
Treat NULL as 100
questions.explanation: WHERE retains TRUE, not UNKNOWN.

questions.question_text: Which predicate selects missing scores?
options: score = NULL
score <> NULL
score IS NULL
score = 0
questions.explanation: IS NULL is the absence test.

questions.question_text: Why is a recorded zero different from a NULL score?
options: Both always mean failure
NULL automatically equals zero
Zero removes an attribute
Zero is a known value; NULL marks absence under the defined contract
questions.explanation: Replacing absence with zero changes meaning.

questions.question_text: What does SELECT score + 5 do to stored scores?
options: It computes output values without updating stored rows
It permanently adds five
It deletes NULL rows
It changes the schema
questions.explanation: An ordinary SELECT expression does not modify source values.

questions.question_text: An INSERT omits a nullable column and receives a default NULL. Is the stored row narrower?
options: Yes; its degree decreases
No; the schema still defines that column
Yes; it becomes a separate relation
Only if the table is empty
questions.explanation: Input omission is not structural omission from the stored row.

questions.question_text: When can two differing complete rows still violate an identity rule?
options: Only when all columns are identical
Whenever they share a programme
When they share a value that must be unique as a key
Only when they are adjacent
questions.explanation: A key constraint can reject rows that differ outside the key.

questions.question_text: What should a missing/pass/fail CASE expression distinguish explicitly?
options: Physical row positions
Insertion timestamps only
Column widths
Missing scores from recorded failing scores
questions.explanation: Absence and failure are different states in the stated contract.

coding_problems.title: Find student facts with missing scores
coding_problems.task: Return student_id and student_name for students whose score is missing. Preserve separate identities with repeated names.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, student_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, score INT NULL);
constraints: Identifiers are unique; supplied scores are NULL or integers from 0 to 100.
edge_cases: Repeated student names identify separate students.
A recorded zero must not be treated as missing.
hints: Retain the identifier in the output.
Handle NULL explicitly before ordinary numeric comparisons.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT student_id, student_name FROM students WHERE score IS NULL ORDER BY student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The result preserves one row per qualifying student and interprets missing scores separately from known scores.

coding_problems.title: Classify each student score
coding_problems.task: Return student_id and score_status for every student: missing for NULL, pass for score >= 50, otherwise below. Use lowercase labels.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, student_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, score INT NULL);
coding_problems.expected:
student_id	score_status
1	missing
2	below
3	pass
4	below
constraints: Identifiers are unique; supplied scores are NULL or integers from 0 to 100.
edge_cases: Repeated student names identify separate students.
A recorded zero must not be treated as missing.
hints: Retain the identifier in the output.
Handle NULL explicitly before ordinary numeric comparisons.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT student_id, CASE WHEN score IS NULL THEN 'missing' WHEN score >= 50 THEN 'pass' ELSE 'below' END AS score_status FROM students ORDER BY student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The result preserves one row per qualifying student and interprets missing scores separately from known scores.
